I will never forget the feeling I had the first time I met my boyfriend’s sons. I was at a Super Bowl party, and we had been dating for about six months. He walked in with them, and the way he interacted with his boys made my heart soar. It was even sweeter when one of them, still wearing the jersey of the team that had just lost, sat there embarrassed and quiet. My boyfriend didn’t tease him out of  his disappointment. He didn’t perform for the room. He just consoled him with a “You got this, buddy!” attitude, the way a father does when he knows a boy’s confidence has taken a hit and needs a steady hand more than a speech or even a hug.

Highlights

Too many people today talk as if fathers are simply second mothers—as if a family is just two interchangeable adults dividing tasks on a spreadsheet.

He’s the most involved father I’ve ever seen in my life. Not because he tries to prove a point or show off but because it is who he is. He cooks. He cleans. He cares. The time and energy that he gives his children goes far beyond the bills he covers.

That Super Bowl night stays with me because it captured something our culture keeps getting wrong. We’re living through a genuine shift in family life. Research shows that fathers are more engaged at home and with their children than any generation of men before them. Data from the Institute for Family Studies and other researchers finds that married dads of young children now spend far more hours on child care and housework than their counterparts did in the 1960s. College-educated fathers in particular have increased the time they spend on child care by hours each week. Like I keep drilling home, the old sitcom dad who hides behind a newspaper while Mom does everything else is out of touch. In a two-income economy, men have taken on more of the daily work of raising children.

That change is, in many families, a necessity. It’s also a gift. Involved fathers are good for children, mothers, and communities. Children with married, engaged dads have stronger self-regulation, fewer behavioral problems, better language development, and a clearer path into adulthood. Boys are less likely to fall into trouble. Girls with present and involved fathers in the home are less likely to experience loneliness, confidence issues, and depression. 

Fathers play differently than mothers. They roughhouse more. They push a little harder. They open the world. That’s the point of fatherhood.

So yes, celebrate the dad with the baby carrier. Celebrate the dad who knows which sippy cup his toddler will actually drink from. Celebrate the man who can build a career and still sit on the floor after a heartbreaking Super Bowl. We should be shouting this from the rooftops.

But here’s the problem I can’t shake off: Too many people now talk as if fathers are simply second mothers. As if a family is just two interchangeable adults dividing tasks on a spreadsheet. As if the highest compliment you can give a man is that he parents “just like a Mom.” I agree with many of the points in a recent piece from The Independent, “Caring fathers aren’t ‘soft’—they’re showing us a new kind of strength,” but it is framed as “dads can be just like moms, and that’s strength.” They don’t mention the ways dads are strong as men.

The more we pretend that fathers are the same as mothers, the more we damage the relationship between men and women.

Let’s be clear: Fathers are not mothers. It’s very important in our changing times that we keep that distinction clear.    .

My friend Carlo in Brooklyn has a young daughter, and on the weekends, he’s always the parent who takes her to her ballet lessons. He tells me he isn’t the only dad there; in fact, it’s often the dads who bring their daughters to lessons on Saturdays. He says the guys love it, as it gives them a chance to connect and bond. This is a great way to integrate father presence without dads pretending to be moms. They give their time in the best way, cheer on their daughters, and get to be men at the same time.

I watched one of the late Gloria Steinem’s last interviews. It was the most frustrated I’ve ever felt listening to a conversation. Not only did she seem completely out-of-touch with the challenges we’re facing today between men and women—challenges her work has significantly contributed to—but she kept emphasizing that men and women have no differences, we’re just all humans. She lit up describing how many men now wear baby carriers and push strollers. She treated it as proof that men are the same as women and this sameness is a great advance for society.

But parents are not interchangeable, like Steinem implied. Equal dignity and more balanced time spent in care isn’t the same as identical function! We chant “gender equality now” until the moment reality walks in the room. Watch what happens in war or natural disasters. Suddenly nobody is confused about the difference between men and women. Nature remembers what this ideology forgot.

The more we pretend that fathers are the same as mothers, the more we damage the relationship between men and women. Families don’t thrive on sameness. They thrive on complementarity: two people bringing different strengths to the same beloved work. When we erase the idea of those differences, we don’t get fairness. We get confusion, resentment, and a quiet sense that neither parent, man nor woman, is allowed to be fully themselves.

Families need the masculine energy fathers bring: the play that borders on risk, the expectation that a child can handle more than they think, the presence that says I will stand between you and the world if I have to, and the authority figure that makes children, in particular boys, respect authority in the future. Studies show children even react to a man’s voice differently in this context. Mothers bring something no policy paper can gaslight. When we tell fathers to parent as if they were mothers, we don’t elevate fatherhood. We diminish motherhood and fatherhood. We treat womanhood as the default human setting and manhood as a costume that should be removed for the good of the children.

This doesn’t stop at the nursery or playroom, either. The modern economy is increasingly built around traits and sectors that lean female. The job categories still growing are the ones women already dominate: education, healthcare, administration, and the caring professions. Commentators look at those fields and announce that we need more men in them. And I agree! Boys need male teachers. Patients benefit from male nurses. Families need men in the institutions that shape the next generation, and where the jobs actually are.

But the reason we need men in those professions is because masculine energy belongs there, too. A male teacher helps a restless boy by being a man the boy can watch, test himself against, and trust. For decades, we have tried to explain this with the nicest possible lie: that men and women are the same, and any leftover difference is a social error to be fixed, not nature at work. 

But fathers are not mothers. Men and women were never meant to be rivals, and we were never meant to be copies of each other. We are on the same team. The team works best when each player is allowed to bring what only he or shecan naturally bring, and that’s how we build strong families.

Lisa Britton is a Contributing Writer at IFS who covers gender issues and family life. Her work has been shared by members of Congress, presidential candidates, a First Lady, and the President of the United States. She has been featured in national publications including Newsweek, LA Times, and the Washington Examiner.
